title: How to Hide (and Actually Repair) Stucco Cracks
description: Not every stucco crack is cosmetic. How to read crack patterns, which ones you can patch and coat, and when a crack needs an engineer before any paint.
excerpt: How to tell cosmetic stucco cracks from serious ones, and the right way to patch, bridge, and coat them so they stay hidden.
h1: How to Hide (and Actually Repair) Stucco Cracks
heroIntro: Painting over a stucco crack hides it for a month or two. Then it reappears, right where it was. To make it disappear for good, you have to know what kind of crack it is and match the repair to the movement behind it.

secondary: when to worry about stucco cracks
questions: Are hairline cracks in stucco normal?
Can you paint over stucco cracks?
When should I worry about cracks in stucco?

sections.h2: Read the crack before you fix it
body: Different forces leave different crack patterns, and each calls for a different repair.
bullets: Map or spiderweb cracking: fine, random hairlines across a wall. Usually shrinkage as the stucco cured. Generally cosmetic.
Diagonal cracks at window and door corners: stress concentrates at openings. Common and usually minor if narrow, but they can move with the seasons.
Straight horizontal or vertical lines: often follow framing, sheathing joints, or the joint between block and wood frame. They tend to open and close with temperature and moisture.
Stair-step cracks along block joints and cracks that are wider at one end: may indicate settlement or foundation movement.
Cracks with bulging, hollow-sounding, or loose stucco around them: possible moisture behind the wall or loss of bond to the lath or block.

sections.h2: When a crack needs more than paint
body: Measure and monitor before you repair. A credit card is a handy gauge: hairlines too thin to fit an edge into are typically cosmetic. Cracks roughly 1/8 inch and wider, cracks that are growing, cracks with one side offset from the other, and doors or windows that have started to stick all deserve a closer look. Pencil a short line at each end of the crack with the date and check it after a few weeks.

If a crack is widening, offset, or accompanied by interior cracking or sticking doors, have a structural engineer or a qualified foundation professional evaluate it before any cosmetic repair. Coating a moving structural crack only hides a problem that needs to be understood first. North Central Florida also has karst geology, so unusual or rapidly changing cracking is worth taking seriously rather than painting over.
For fine cracks that are not moving, the goal is to seal them and make them invisible under the finish.
bullets: Clean the wall with a gentle wash and let it dry fully.
Brush out loose material from the crack.
Work an elastomeric patching compound or a brush-grade crack filler into the crack, and feather it flush.
Match the texture with a sponge, brush, or texture compound so the patch blends with the surrounding stucco.
Prime patched areas with a masonry primer if the product calls for it, then apply the finish coats.
Open the crack slightly with a grinder or chisel into a shallow V so the repair material has room to bond.
Clean and dampen as the patch manufacturer directs.
Fill with a flexible, paintable sealant for joints that will keep moving, or a stucco patch for wider static cracks.
For recurring cracks, embed fiberglass mesh in a base coat over the repair to spread the stress.
Re-texture to match and allow full cure.
Coat with an elastomeric wall system that can stretch over minor movement.

sections.h2: Why patches show through the paint
body: Even a sound repair can stand out once the wall is painted. Two things cause it. First, texture: a smooth patch on a sand-finish or knockdown wall catches light differently, especially when the sun rakes across it in the morning or late afternoon. Take time to match the texture, and step back to look at it from an angle before priming. Second, porosity: fresh patching material absorbs paint differently from the surrounding stucco, so a single coat over it can dry with a different sheen or shade, an effect painters call flashing. Priming the patches and applying full coats over the entire wall, corner to corner, rather than dabbing paint on the repairs, evens it out.

This is also why spot-painting old stucco rarely blends. Paint on the rest of the wall has faded and chalked, so even the original color mixed fresh will not match. If the wall needs several repairs, plan to repaint the whole elevation.

sections.h2: Why elastomeric coatings help, and when they do not
body: Elastomeric coatings are thick, rubbery films that can bridge hairline cracks and flex as the wall moves, which makes them a strong choice for stucco with ongoing hairline movement. They need to be applied at the specified thickness to work, which usually means more material per square foot than ordinary paint.

They are not a cure-all. They are less breathable than standard acrylics, so applying them over a wall that is already wet can trap moisture and cause blistering. Check moisture first, fix any leaks, and make sure the stucco is sound. On walls without crack issues, a quality 100% acrylic is often the better match. For more on stucco specifically, see our stucco repair and painting service.

Much stucco cracking is driven by the ground beneath. Keep downspouts discharging well away from the house, maintain a positive slope away from the foundation, and avoid irrigation spraying the base of walls, so the foundation is not cycling between soaked and dry. Seal around penetrations and window perimeters, and repaint before the old coating chalks and cracks so water is not soaking into bare stucco. Columbia County homeowners will find region-specific detail in our article on stucco cracks in Lake City homes.

Sealing a few hairlines on a single-story wall is a reasonable DIY job. Use a product labeled for exterior stucco, work in the shade on a dry day, and expect to repaint the whole wall afterward so the repairs blend in. Avoid high-pressure washing beforehand, which can erode soft stucco and widen cracks. Matching texture across a large area, repairing wider cracks, working at height, and applying elastomeric systems at the proper thickness are where professional crews earn their keep. faqs.q: Are hairline cracks in stucco normal?
faqs.a: Fine hairline cracks are common, often from shrinkage during curing, and are usually cosmetic. Monitor them, and look closer at any crack that widens, offsets, or keeps returning.

faqs.q: Can I just paint over stucco cracks?
faqs.a: Regular paint will crack again along the same line. Clean and fill the crack first, match the texture, and use an elastomeric coating if the wall has ongoing hairline movement.

faqs.q: When should I worry about a stucco crack?
faqs.a: Worry about cracks wider than about 1/8 inch, cracks that are growing or offset, stair-step patterns in block, or cracks with sticking doors and windows. Have those evaluated before repair.

faqs.q: Is elastomeric paint good for stucco?
faqs.a: It works well on stucco with hairline cracking because it stretches and bridges small cracks. It should go on a dry, sound wall at the specified thickness.
